sections.markdown:
## C — Night and inclement weather: seeing after dark, headlights and glare, parking at night, rain, fog and smoke, slippery roads, hydroplaning, skids, running off the pavement, flooding, wind and winter braking
Knowledge domain: how to drive safely in Tennessee after dark and in bad weather — why night is riskier, how to use, aim and dim headlights and recover from glare, how to park at night, how to adjust for rain, fog and smoke, where roads turn slick, how to handle hydroplaning, skids and wheels off the pavement, why floodwater is deadly, and how to handle wind, ice and snow.

FACT_ID: sec11-F01 | anchor: A01
Night driving is especially risky on poorly lit highways and country roads, because you see clearly over a much shorter distance and dark animals, cars and people in dark clothing are hard to spot. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec11-F02 | anchor: A01
Even though traffic is lighter at night, the chance of a serious crash is much greater than during the day. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec11-F03 | anchor: A01
Most of a driver's reaction time depends on eyesight, and depth perception, color recognition and side vision all weaken after dark. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec11-F04 | anchor: A01
More fatal crashes happen on Friday and Saturday nights than on any other day of the week. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec11-F05 | anchor: A01
The basic rule of night driving is never to outrun your headlights, which means driving slowly enough to stop within the distance your lights show you. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec11-F06 | anchor: A01
At night, keep your stopping distance shorter than your sight distance and weigh how strong your lights are and how well your brakes respond. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec11-F07 | anchor: A01
Look beyond the reach of your headlight beams for dark shapes, and glance left and right now and then to locate the pavement edge and oncoming cars. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec11-F08 | anchor: A01
Do not look straight into oncoming headlights, which can blind you for a moment; instead watch the right edge of the road and steer by the white edge line. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec11-F09 | anchor: A01
Do not flash your high beams to warn another driver, because it can distract that driver and lead to a crash. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec11-F10 | anchor: A01
Tennessee law requires headlights that let you clearly see a person on the highway at least 200 feet ahead, so they must work properly, be aimed correctly and have clean lenses. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec11-F11 | anchor: A01
Glare recovery time is the pause after an oncoming car passes while your narrowed pupils adjust back to dim light, and during it you are close to driving blind. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec11-F12 | anchor: A01
Glare recovery time does not depend on how sharp your eyesight is; it differs from person to person and is usually worse for older drivers and people in poor physical condition. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec11-F13 | anchor: A01
To fight glare, keep the windshield clear on both sides along with your eyeglasses, and clean your headlights and windows inside and out at least once a month. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec11-F14 | anchor: A01
Headlights pointed too high or too far outward do not help you see the road; they only add glare for drivers you meet or follow. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec11-F15 | anchor: A01
Switch to low beams whenever you meet an oncoming vehicle or come up behind one within 500 feet. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec11-F16 | anchor: A01
Use low beams at all times when driving in cities and towns, and avoid blasting an oncoming driver with high beams on curves or turns to the right. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec11-F17 | anchor: A02
Never leave your headlights on while parked at night, even briefly, because a stopped car's lights can blind approaching drivers and mislead them about where the road runs. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec11-F18 | anchor: A02
Whenever you park on or beside a highway at night, leave your emergency flashers and parking lights on. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec11-F19 | anchor: A02
Wet pavement can be as dangerous as ice, so slow down at the first sign of rain, since you will need more stopping distance and may skid on sharp turns. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec11-F20 | anchor: A02
Roads are usually most slippery right after rain begins, because dirt and oil mix with the water into a greasy film that robs your tires of grip. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec11-F21 | anchor: A02
In fog or mist, use low beams and never high beams, because high-beam light bounces back into your eyes. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec11-F22 | anchor: A02
The best advice for fog or smoke is not to drive in it; Tennessee can see forest-fire smoke and temperature-driven fog in any season. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec11-F23 | anchor: A02
If you must drive in fog or smoke, use low beams, never drive with only parking lights or fog lights on, and reduce your speed. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec11-F24 | anchor: A02
If you cannot see the edge of the road in fog, pull off far to the right, completely clear of the travel lane, and switch on your emergency flashers. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec11-F25 | anchor: A02
Tennessee law requires you to turn on low-beam headlights when driving in daylight through dense fog, heavy rain or snow, which also helps oncoming drivers see you. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec11-F26 | anchor: A03
Hydroplaning happens when heavy water makes your tires lose all contact with the pavement, so a small steering change or a gust of wind can send the car into a skid or spin. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec11-F27 | anchor: A03
If your vehicle starts to hydroplane, slow down gradually by easing off the gas, and do not slam on the brakes. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec11-F28 | anchor: A03
Hydroplaning can triple your stopping distance and reduce or eliminate steering control. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec11-F29 | anchor: A03
Hydroplaning is more likely at higher speeds, but tires can hydroplane at any speed under the right conditions. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec11-F30 | anchor: A03
Skids happen when the tires can no longer grip the road, and they are caused by drivers going too fast for conditions. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec11-F31 | anchor: A03
In a skid, stay off the brake and steer in the direction you want the car to go; if the rear slides to the left, steer to the left. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec11-F32 | anchor: A03
If your wheels drop off the paved road, lift your foot off the gas without braking suddenly and keep a firm grip without jerking the wheel back toward the pavement. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec11-F33 | anchor: A03
After running off the pavement, brake lightly and briefly instead of slamming or holding the pedal, and steer back on only once nearby traffic is clear and you have slowed. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec11-F34 | anchor: A03
Each year flooding kills more people than any other thunderstorm hazard, and many victims are drivers who try to cross flooded roads. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec11-F35 | anchor: A03
Just six inches of fast-moving floodwater can knock a person down, and moving water of 18 to 24 inches deep is enough to sweep away most cars. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec11-F36 | anchor: A03
Turn Around, Don't Drown: stay out of flooded roads, because the water may be much deeper than it looks where the roadbed has washed out. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec11-F37 | anchor: A04
A driver who knowingly ignores clearly visible flood warning signs or barricades and drives into a flooded road can be charged with reckless driving and made to repay the cost of the rescue. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec11-F38 | anchor: A04
If you spot a tornado, do not try to outrun it; get out of the car, find a ditch or low spot and lie face down to protect yourself from flying debris. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec11-F39 | anchor: A04
When a large truck or bus passes you on the left, move as far right in your lane as you can and slow down to handle its wind gusts. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec11-F40 | anchor: A05
On snow or ice, continuous hard braking can lock the front wheels and take away your steering control. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec11-F41 | anchor: A05
On snow or ice, brake firmly to just short of lockup, ease off slightly if the wheels lock, then reapply and hold steady pressure without pumping. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec11-F42 | anchor: A05
With antilock brakes, keep constant, firm pressure on the pedal, and in an emergency stop push it all the way to the floor if needed, even on wet or icy roads. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0092]

Misconceptions: lighter night traffic does not make night driving safer; high beams make fog worse, not better; a heavy car or truck does not stay grounded in moving floodwater; braking in a skid or while hydroplaning makes it worse; pumping the brakes is not the right way to stop on ice; jerking the wheel straight back after running off the pavement is dangerous.
Mnemonics: never outrun your headlights; low beams in fog, rain and snow; Turn Around, Don't Drown; steer where you want to go; overpower, over-brake, over-steer are the snow and ice errors.
Glossary: glare recovery time means the interval for your eyes to readjust after bright headlights pass; hydroplaning means tires riding on water instead of the road; skid means tires losing grip on the road; rumble stripe means an edge line painted over shallow indentations; antilock brakes means a system that keeps wheels from locking so you can steer.
Dynamic facts: the daytime low-beam rule, the headlight distance requirement, the reckless driving charge and rescue-cost rule for ignoring flood barricades, and the dimming distance are set by Tennessee law and can change; confirm them on official Tennessee sources before showing them to learners.

corpus_stability.reason: The Tennessee Comprehensive Driver License Manual says its content is current as of July 1, 2022 and its back cover carries one March 2025 print authorization; nothing in the selected pages suggests more than one rewrite per year, but the content date is old, so freshness is held as debt rather than assumed.
